title: DNS-Based Routing, TTLs, and GeoDNS
lesson:
The Domain Name System maps names to IP addresses, and because every client resolves names before connecting, DNS is a cheap place to steer traffic. A single name can return multiple A or AAAA records (round-robin DNS), or the authoritative server can choose answers per query: GeoDNS returns the endpoint nearest the resolver's location, weighted records split traffic by percentage, and health-checked records drop endpoints that fail probes. This is how many systems send users to the closest region or fail over between regions.

Every DNS answer carries a time-to-live (TTL) that tells resolvers how long they may cache it. A long TTL cuts query load and latency but means changes propagate slowly; a short TTL lets you shift traffic or fail over quickly but increases query volume and makes you more dependent on the DNS provider's availability. A common practice is to lower the TTL ahead of a planned migration, make the change, and raise it again afterward.

DNS-based routing has real limits. Resolvers and clients may cache beyond the TTL, so failover is never instantaneous and some users keep hitting a dead endpoint for minutes. GeoDNS sees the recursive resolver's address rather than the end user's, so a user on a distant public resolver may be routed to a suboptimal region unless the resolver supports EDNS Client Subnet. DNS also has no view of per-connection load, so it balances coarsely.

Because of this, DNS is typically the outer layer of a layered design: DNS or anycast steers users to a region, and inside the region a load balancer does fine-grained, connection-aware balancing and fast health checking. Treat DNS as a slow, coarse control plane rather than a real-time traffic switch.

questions.prompt: Why is DNS-based failover slower than load-balancer failover?
options: DNS cannot return more than one IP
Resolvers and clients cache answers for up to the TTL, and sometimes longer
Load balancers use a different IP protocol
questions.explanation: Cached answers keep pointing at the failed endpoint until the TTL (or a misbehaving cache) expires.

questions.prompt: Lowering a record's TTL before a planned migration lets the change take effect sooner once you make it.
questions.explanation: Resolvers will have cached the old answer only for the short TTL, so they pick up the new one quickly.

questions.prompt: A DNS setup that returns the endpoint nearest the requester's resolver is called ____ routing.
questions.explanation: GeoDNS picks answers based on the location of the querying resolver.

questions.prompt: A user on a distant public DNS resolver is routed to a far-away region. What is the most likely cause?
options: The authoritative server sees the resolver's address, not the user's
The record was an AAAA record
questions.explanation: GeoDNS geolocates the resolver unless EDNS Client Subnet passes along part of the client's address.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a low-risk DNS cutover to a new endpoint, earliest first.
items: Raise the TTL back to its normal value
Update the record to the new endpoint
Lower the TTL and wait for the old TTL to expire
Verify traffic is healthy on the new endpoint
questions.explanation: Shortening the TTL first makes the switch propagate fast, and the TTL is restored only after the new endpoint is confirmed healthy.
